extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, educators and researchers interested in misinformation and media literacy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for identifying, evaluating, and combating 'fake news' (misinformation/disinformation) in news and social media, including fact‑checking practices, platform interventions, behavioral countermeasures, and research approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to spot fake news (general guides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical how-to guides aimed at readers to help them recognise false or misleading news stories (examples cited: IFLA 'How to spot fake news', FactCheck.org 'How to spot fake news', Time 'Schoolkids taught to identify fake news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These guides typically explain heuristics for readers (check sources, verify claims, look for corroboration, inspect URLs/branding, check publication date and author). The page cites multiple such guides as resources but does not list step-by-step items in this chunk; consult the referenced guides (IFLA, FactCheck.org, Time) for concrete checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) code of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal set of principles governing fact-checking organisations (referenced as 'International Fact-Checking Network fact-checkers' code of principles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a professional standard for fact-checkers (e.g., commitments to nonpartisanship, transparency of sources and funding, methodology disclosure). The page references the IFCN code as a benchmark for credible fact‑checking operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher fact-checking methodology (The Conversation example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet-level descriptions of how individual news organisations perform fact checks (example cited: 'How we do fact checks at The Conversation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that credible outlets document their fact-checking procedures and criteria (what they verify, sourcing standards, how corrections are handled). Use such documented methodologies to judge the reliability of a fact-check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field guides to fake-news sites and hoax purveyors (Snopes example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference guides that catalog known fake-news and hoax sites and explain common deceptive tactics (example cited: 'Snopes' field guide to fake news sites and hoax purveyors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for identifying repeat offenders and understanding site-level signals of fakery (e.g., mimicry of real outlets, monetisation patterns). The page points readers to these reference lists as detection aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing disinformation, misinformation, and propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual criteria for classifying false information by intent and mechanism (referenced: 'Distinguishing disinformation from propaganda, misinformation, and "fake news"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages evaluators to consider intent (deliberate vs. accidental), origin (state actors, troll farms, pranksters), and function (propaganda, satire, error) when judging content. The page cites work that clarifies these distinctions as an evaluative framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prebunking / inoculation strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive interventions that prepare audiences to resist misinformation by exposing them to misleading techniques or by boosting accurate cues (references include 'What Is Prebunking?', van der Linden 'Inoculating against misinformation', and research on accuracy-nudge interventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a quality/impact criterion for interventions: effective prebunking explains rhetorical tricks and provides factual forewarning; studies cited (e.g., accuracy‑nudge experiments) indicate these can reduce belief in false headlines. Use prebunking as a recommended practice in media literacy programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral/UX interventions to reduce sharing (accuracy nudges, prompts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform-level behavioural nudges designed to reduce the spread of false content (examples cited: 'read before you retweet' prompts on Twitter, Facebook flags/warnings, partnerships with fact-checkers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criteria include whether interventions prompt users to consider accuracy, reduce impulsive sharing, and are scalable. The page references empirical work showing deliberation can reduce belief in false headlines and platform trials of prompts/flags as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated fake-news detection research
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational/data-mining approaches to detect false news on social media (cited: 'Fake news detection on social media: A data mining perspective' and related research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a technical rubric for automated systems: features used (linguistic signals, propagation patterns, source networks), performance trade-offs, and limitations; the page cites this literature as an evidence base rather than giving a single prescriptive algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation, bans, and policy responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies and enforcement actions by platforms and governments to limit misinformation (examples in the text: Facebook/Google partnerships with fact-checkers, bans of accounts or removal of content, Google funding to fight fake news, arrests and legal actions in multiple countries for spreading 'fake news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative considerations include proportionality, effect on freedom of expression, potential for abuse (censorship), and effectiveness at limiting harm. The page documents both platform measures and government responses, noting tensions between control and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and civic consequences framework
rubrics_metrics.description: References to legal actions and arrests for spreading false information (numerous country-level examples during COVID-19) indicating a regulatory/penal approach to fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing responses to misinformation, consider legal standards (what constitutes punishable falsehood), human-rights implications, due process, and the risk of misuse against dissent. The page cites cases showing these risks across jurisdictions.
